speechtext: There is a reduction in the expenditure.
Is it corresponding?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
For purposes of comparison it might be well for me to give the figures for the last three years. The general office expense, including travelling expenses of inspectors and appraisers for 19211922 was $285,777.23; 1922-23, $200,700; for 1923-1924 estimated $180,000, Salaries exclusive of agricultural supervision for 1921-1922, $823,189.26; 1922-23, $711,600; 1923-1924, estimated $500,000. Legal expenses and disbursements, 1921-1922, $37,220.23; 1922-1923, $28,000; 1923-1924, estimated $20,000. Printing and stationery, 1921-1922, $32,022.88;	1922-1923,
$27,300; 1923-1924, estimated' $20,000. Advertising, 1921-1922, $5,190.39; 1922-1923, $3,600; 1923-1924, estimated $3,000. Miscellaneous, 1921-1922, $2,418.55; 1922-1923, $7,600; 19231924, estimated $5,000; making totals of expenditure for the three years respectively $1,185,818.54, $978,800, and $728,000. The figures for agricultural expenditure-will the totals satisfy my hon. friend?
I think so now.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Agricultural expenditure including salaries, travelling expenses, motor car accessories, and home branch courses, for 1921-1922, $869,525.45; for 19221923, $695,900; for 1923-1924, estimated $672,000. Now I will give the totals of all these items; 1921-1922,	$2,055,343.99;	1922-1923,
$1,674,700; and for 1923-1924, estimated $1,400,000.

The reduction is far from a corresponding reduction. The number of soldiers now being placed on the land is relatively negligible, but the cost is keeping up pretty well. Of course, I admit that in respect to the supervision work that would not be expected to contract very much. The minister's figures show a very small diminution from last year and the year before, but I would not criticize that. I would think that only a small diminution could be made, but I really think that as to the rest, the amount of machinery and the expenditure of the organization is away beyond the actual work being performed. It would seem to me that way. Could I get these particulars, for example? The minister gave the figures for legal costs. They seem to be keeping up magnificently. Could the minister tell us how many loans were made on land in 1922-1923,

and the cost per loan, also how many were made on land, say, in the year 1919-1920, and the cost per loan? I was in charge at that time, and I know we made very stringent rules as to legal costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The explanation that I get for the legal fees is that this seems to be a sort of continuing business ; that is it is not cleaned up in the years in which the men are established but goes on from year to year. I am informed that some of the legal business even of 1919 is stili unfinished in that respect.
In answer to my right hon. friend's criticism as to reductions in the staff I may say that one could expect that there would be a reasonable reduction in the inside staff.
In so far as the outside inspection is concerned, however, I am rather of the opinion that until these settlers are firmly established they will require supervision. It would not be good business because of the mere fact that you are not settling very many men to reduce the field inspectors or the officers who are supervising the work of these men.
I admit that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think that is the strongest feature of the whole scheme. Indeed, I would go as far as to say that if these men were withdrawn we would perhaps have a great many more salvage cases than we otherwise would have. On the other hand, in making inquiry from the board with respect to the probable cost of carrying on the soldier settlement work-that is provided we could reduce the field staff, the agricul * tural staff, or the inspectional staff almost -to -a minimum-I am informed that the cost of collections and of the general work of the staff necessary to carry on the salvage work, and of their salaries, will amount. to a very considerable sum. In all probability it will take more than half a million dollars annually to carry it along. That may seem to be rather a large figure for that kind of work, but there is jjot any doubt that a very large amount of salvage work is required in connection with carrying out this scheme. That is very evident now, although an adjustment last year has had the effect of reducing it very materially. I think I have the figures in that connection. I do not think, however, it will be possible to make a success of this work by making a very serious reduction in the -inspectional staff, or a reduction beyond a reasonable number for the carrying out of the scheme in its entirety until such times, at least, as these men have more than half

Supply-Soldiers' Settlement
paid up the loans they received from the government.

In what I said before T admitted what the minister had said that the supervisory work-which, as he well remarks is one of the best features of the whole plan- cannot be contracted proportionately at all to the contraction of the placing of men. Indeed, I do not think it can be done very rapidly at all. I fancy that it would be bad policy to look for a rapid reduction in the staff of professors, collectors, and instructors, but what I had reference to were other expenses. For example, I could not understand why now-as against two or three years ago when we were placing at the rate of 10,090 men a year on the land and the legal expenses were under some 830,000-when we are placing almost none those expenses still keep up to about 820,000. That did not seem reasonable to me. The minister is informed that the legal fees drag on. Well, they will if they are allowed to. For the life of me I do not know why they should.
That is the bad feature of the legal business.

Yes, and there is need for control by a strong hand. As to the loans that were made in 1919-20 there would not b -a loan made until the title was passed. It is true that the matter might drag until this year but it would not be in the 1919-20 loans; it would be in the loans this year. The loans would not be made until the title was passed. There might be cause why the title could not be passed and it might drag on to this year, but that would not be counted in the loans for 1919-20. I think we had a comparison of the cost per loan in 1919-20. We had it figured out and it was all, I think, given to the House; it was very low indeed. I would like to see if it is the same for last year, when probably another class of lawyers got in and handled the soldier settlement work.
While I am on my feet I wish to express gratification at the results considering all the conditions under which this work has been conducted. The whole soldier settlement scheme encountered just about as heavy obstacles as any plan ever launched by the administration encountered. No one, who was not through it, can realize fully the pressure that was brought upon the government after the return of those hundreds of thousands of men-pressure for one form of enterprise one day, another form of enterprise the next; very heavy pressure for entering upon a scheme of land purchase and loans for the purpose of colonizing the returned

soldiers. It was indeed a dangerous enterprise; there was risk at every comer. I do not think any government launched anything in which it was more difficult to select sound and true lines in order to avoid error-I had almost said at a thousand points-in entering upon that work. It encountered a diminution in land values. That is, perhaps, the biggest obstacle the work has faced. Well, it has gone through that. Concessions had to be made because of that-concessions made a year ago which I think were right. They were very simple; they merely meant a grant out of the treasury, that was all; it was not a very great one. But when we consider that obstacle, when we consider as well, and associated with it, the lowering of farm prices not accompanied by any lowering of farm costs proportionately-when we consider that while the soldier settlement scheme, a new scheme, has to be made to go while farming, in general becomes more and more a matter of standing still, of loss rather than of gain, and that through it all this scheme survives to a very satisfactory degree of success, I think it indeed reflects credit on those who worked it out; and I am not saying this without mentioning the man who chiefly did it. The loans were mainly devised by Dr. Black, now the minister's deputy for the Department of Immigration; and the soundness of the policies adopted, the various safeguards instituted, and the strong features that have saved it through these very difficult years, are attributable to the good judgment of Dr. Black. Now, I merely say that had the years been even years -that is to say had conditions been normal; when we put in the work we could not wait, we had to do it then, there was no option on our part-had they remained the same in the matter of land value, in the matter of farm sale prices, and farm purchase prices, then unquestionably the whole soldier settlement organization to-day, and the men who have been placed on land under it, would be a very pronounced success. At the present time I think it can be said that the soldier farmer, taking all things into consideration, is in a better position relative to that in which he was when he started than the other farmer relative to the position he was in at the same time. I do not think there is any dispute about that. Consequently the scheme has been a success, and if we have an improvement in time, which I look for myself, then the whole advantage that this country has any right to expect will be harvested. I only hope I can get the figures of the cost, because I would like to be sure that it is being run on the same economic

Supply-Soldiers' Settlement

principle and being watched as carefully as it was some years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: With regard to the legal part, I think perhaps my hon. friend is expecting too much of a reduction in the legal costs, owing to the fact that we were not establishing as many men as we were in the years he speaks of. The legal officers are on salary. This applies to Ontario, Quebec and the eastern provinces, but not to the West, and there is a considerable amount of salvage. True there is perhaps not a great amount of legal fees involved in the matter, still there are bound to be more or less legal costs, and the board must protect themselves against any action that might be taken against them for various causes. I can only assure my hon. friend that we will exercise the utmost caution in connection *with these fees that are paid to solicitors. The chairman informs me that exactly the same fees are being paid as were paid formerly.
The same scale?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, same scale.
I have every confidence in the chairman. He has been a lawyer himself, and could not be imposed on unless he comes under the malign influences of party favoritism.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Having had considerable experience in farming, I am not unmindful of the fact that in establishing a soldier upon the land, making the loans that have been made and will no doubt be made in the future, considerable care will have to be exercised to keep out of difficulty, and I am of the opinion that due care should be exercised in connection with every loan made, as well as due care exercised when salvage cases occur, and they are occurring to a considerable extent. But I will tell my hon. friend that I do not want to be criticized by him, and I am willing to give him and the Conservative party full credit for instituting the establishment of the soldiers upon the land. I do not want to interfere in any way with the scheme, and I wish to assure him that I think the board to a man would be prepared to say that in no way have I myself interfered, or permitted anyone else to interfere, with the settlement of a single man or made any suggestion in regard to it. I have not interfered in any way. I have simply allowed the board to carry on as they have been doing in the past. In other words, I have left it entirely to the discretion of the board in dealing with these cases.
Who selects the legal men in the various provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Justice department I am told have made those appointments and that has been the rule, but the fees that are paid are taxed by the members of the Soldiers' Settlement Board, and adjustments made if necesary.
Then the patronage system is still in force in this department, as in other departments?
Being continued.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have no
knowledge of any change, if it was patronage. I wish to assure my hon. friend that I did not know there was any change, and I do not know of any change in the method of selection.

I was very pleased to hear the minister state the policy has not been changed in any shape or form. That is a compliment to my right hon. leader who really originated the scheme, or, at least, as minister put it into effect. I should like to have the minister make some statement as to the general condition of the soldiers now on the land. When the question was before the House last year we discussed the conditions at some length. I well remember that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) described the very serious condition of men in the prairie provinces who were put on the land, and I think it might be well for the minister to give us some idea of the number of men now on the land, as compared with, say, a couple of years ago, and as to their general conditions, of prosperity or the reverse, because I am sure not only the House but the country generally is interested in the question of the soldier settlement scheme as a whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I, perhaps, cannot answer my hon. friend any better than to give him the comparative statement of the financial condition as it appears by our returns. I will be unable to give my hon. friend a statement as to the actual conditions on the land in comparison with a year ago or two years ago.
The minister can tell the condition by the number who wish to get out of the contract which they made. In that way we will be able to get a very good idea as to how they are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will give my hon. friend the report of salvages but I wanted first to give the collections because they are a pretty fair indication of how the

Supply-Soldiers' Settlement
men are progressing. The date of last year's report is April 14th, 1922, and this statement I have before me is from October to April in both years. I am quoting this year's report as against that of last year. Last year the collection was $1,537,158.88 or 37.7 per cent of the amount due. This year, 1923, for the same period, the total is $1,662,778.99, or 55.6 per cent of the amount due. Therefore we have an increase of 37.7 per cent to 55.6 per cent for the same period, which is the heavy collection period.
I would take it that, from the financial statement the minister would probably say that conditions of men on the land are improving. Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. Still, if you take certain areas in Canada, for instance the northern portion of Alberta, while that was fairly prosperous last year, their returns do not show up as well. But the totals, taking Canada as a whole, show that conditions are improving. This is a statement of the totals. No doubt hon. gentlemen will say that the statement does not show up as well as the statement of last year; but as a matter of fact, that is the complete statement.
Will the reductions in payments this year make some difference in those percentages?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is true.

It must be remembered
that, as was to be expected, some returned soldiers were placed on land where they could not succeed, but not through any fault of their own. Take those soldiers and others who had a better chance and who still did not succeed, that is all the class of salvaged soldiers. After they have left their land, what is the policy of the government as regards the debt? I find some of these returned soldiers, after they have been salvaged, are in fear and trembling lest when they start to work elsewhere, their salaries or wages will be garnisheed. I find it is in the contract that they are liable; but in talking with some of the officials of the department, I have heard them say that this debt could not be collected. If it cannot be collected, would it not be wise to cancel the debt entirely and thus free those men from that fear?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The chairman assures me that no man has been pressed for the deficit that may in some cases accrue. In most of the cases upon which I pass, or where salvage has taken place and the resale
of the property has been completed, there is sufficient to cover all the advances made by the board. But there are, of course, and will be a large number of instances in which that will not be the case, in which even after salvage has taken place, the individual will still be a debtor to the government. I would not like to say that in cases where fraud has taken place, we would not pursue; but speaking personally, I would not want to pursue a man who had done his best, but who had made a failure. I do not think that would be a proper thing to do.

Could the minister say positively that in no case any of this debt had been repaid by such returned soldiers? I am not positive; but I think I have heard of at least one case where some part of this debt has been repaid. Again, can we take it from the minister that in every case where a returned soldier has tried to do his best, it will be the policy from now on that he will not be pursued for a return of that debt?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I presume, as long as a man is liable, the act would make it possible to endeavour to collect, if he were able to pay and if it were wise to endeavour to collect. I am simply making the statement personally that unless a man deliberately committed a fraud, if he had made an honest effort and had made a failure, I think it would be very unwise to pursue him for a debt he might owe in that connection.

I should like to ask the minister a question regarding the authority of the supervisors in certain connections. What are the instructions as regards possessing or repossessing a crop? The reason I am asking this question is because certain supervisors have been in my district, for instance, and they have been dictating to these men what debts they shall contract in regard to living. Moreover, I find that on certain farms, they actually possess practically the whole of the crop, with the direct result that these men are not able to pay any store bills. In my particular district, there are three or four returned soldiers who have incurred debts to the local stores, and when they have gone to pay them, they have found that the Soldiers' Settlement Board have taken all the crop and that they cannot pay these debts. The result is that these men are simply getting off the land, not because they feel that they cannot make it pay, but because it is impossible for them to get any more goods at the local stores.
Supply-Soldiers' Settlement

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I had the
same opinion as my hon. friend that, perhaps, there was over-supervision; but one must remember that pretty generous loans were made to these men. I will say very frankly, I think too generous loans were made. That, however, was the judgment of the people who were in charge at that time. 1 am not criticizing that; but I am saying that this increases the responsibilities and it naturally must increase the supervision, because if a man is lent, say, $5,000 or in that vicinity, I mean his total loan, on a quarter section of land, I think a farmer would call that a rather risky loan. Therefore, supervision must play a very important part. That is why I say I think it is important that supervision should continue; and if it appears at times to be of a character that is burdensome, interfering too much even in the home life of the settler, perhaps, after all, in many cases this is for. his good. Instructions, however, are given to the inspectors to use their best judgment. The board inform me that they have had a good many men pass through their hands, and they have now after their experience chosen the men who have shown the better judgment and discretion in dealing with matters of this kind. I have heard the statement made that a settler could not sell a pig; that he could do nothing without the consent of the inspector. We must bear in mind that where a considerable amount of risk is involved in a loan, fairly rigid supervision is necessary.

I am not objecting to the
fairly rigid supervision; but if the supervisor comes and takes all a settler has, you simply force the man out of existence, so that he cannot remain on the land. I can give two instances in my district where they took everything, -when a man had incurred a debt of three or four hundred dollars. I am informed this year from home that the man has removed from the land simply because he cannot live.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
(Argenteuil):	It must
be remembered that there are 22,000 loans. I do not wish it to be understood that I hold any brief for the inspectors. I would rather encourage reasonable judgment being exercised in connection with all these matters; but undoubtedly there wall still be men whom it will be impossible to continue who perhaps are disregarding every advice given by the inspectors, and who find themselves in a serious condition which jeopardizes the loan as well.

Of course I would say that
the crop in that district was not a heavy one,
I Mr. Lewis.]
and the total crop would possibly not more than pay the interest.

I think I have heard
from possibly 400 or 450 of the soldier land settlers in Ontario. Of that vast number I do not think there were more than half a dozen who had any criticism at all to offer concerning the Soldiers' Settlement Board or the work of supervision. It has indeed been very pleasing and encouraging to hear the very hearty approval of the supervisors which the soldiers and their wives in many cases have expressed. While some did say that they rather chafed under the supervision, they felt that the government were only doing what they must do in view of the large amount of money that has been put up, sometimes without any very great security.

I should like to know whether the conditions portrayed by the member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) prevail to any extent now in regard to the settlers who are unable to pay their store bills. We know that this- condition prevailed very largely two years ago, but that was precisely one of the disadvantges which we had hoped to meet by the amendments passed last session when we took the accrued interest and subsidiary loans and consolidated them afresh in a new loan, thus relieving the men of immediate payments. I do not think that the condition the hon. member refers to can be widespread at the present time, because there is practically nothing new save the small first payments. This condition must be considerably relieved since last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Soldiers are only human, like other people in Canada, and there will always be individuals among them who will be improvident, get into debt and run up heavy bills, always of course against the advice of the supervisors. There can be no question about that, and that is one of the things which the supervisors endeavour to keep the settlers from doing. Perhaps they persist in doing it, however, and when adjustment day comes it is quite likely that they feel they are being hardly used. I can quite understand that; but in answer to my hon. friend I would say that so far as I know the condition mentioned has been reduced to the minimum.
Is the minister doing any advertising now for the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have almost ceased to advertise; I believe we are advertising in the veteran papers only.

Supply-Soldiers' Settlement

I have no particular objection to advertising, but I might observe that we did cease it altogether some years ago, because there seemed no need for it; the facts and all the features of the policy were known. What was done years ago was to put in the Veteran and other papers-very few-a mere succinct statement of what the law provided in order that fit men might apply to come in and benefit thereby. But we stopped advertising. The minister, however, revived it, and the reason I became a little doubtful as to what influences were at work was the character of the advertising that he had adopted. It was indeed a remarkable advertisement I saw in one of the papers in which he advertises; this particular advertisement was not of the nature of those inserted when the work was first started, namely, a mere statement of the facts. This was the character of it. In the middle of the page was a letter from a veteran telling how much better tilings were now; he did not have as much to pay this year on account of the legislation of last session, which he used special language to describe; consequently, he was thoroughly well satisfied. Then an explanation was given, at the bottom, of what had ' brought all this about; it was all due to last session's legislation of the present government. In a word, the minister was spending public money to insert a political advertisement, for it was nothing more, because it had nothing whatever to do with the work of the Soldiers' Settlement Board. The advertisement was in a veteran paper which I have filed. There is no question about it; I remember it distinctly, for I was astonished at the character of the advertisement the minister was sending out. It was merely a method of using public money to give political eclat to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Let me assure my hon. friend that this is the first intimation I have had of the letter in question: I did not see it. There has been no increase in advertising in the veteran newspapers or elsewhere. The advertising never ceased; it is just the same as when my right hon. friend had charge of the organization.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is the information I get from the chairman of the board. However, suffice it to say that I have never interfered with the advertising. I want my hon. friend to understand that it is my desire to have this work carried on just as he started it; I want to carry it out in every
detail just as the hon. gentleman originated it. I want to carry it on as economically as I can, and when the time comes that we should curtail expenditure with respect to it I shall be glad to do so. I do not, however, want to be criticized for having interjected into the scheme anything that might interfere with its success; and I have never done so. I have every confidence in the board and I never suggested any advertisement to them. I never knew of this particular advertisement, never solicited it and will not do anything of the kind at any time. I want to give the scheme every chance to succeed, and I can assure my hon. friend that I have no desire to take any political kudos out of it. The hon. gentleman is welcome to it all.

I was not seeking any credit whatever in the matter. I accept the minister's word that he did not father the advertisement, but I am curious to know who did. There must be someone who is attending to that phase of the operations. The minister is wrong, though, when he says that he is merely continuing what wre did in respect of advertising. I cannot say what took place after I left office, but I am quite sure from memory that we ceased advertising. That, however, is not what I object to, if the minister feels that some good can be done by merely letting the returned soldier know what is available for him. If he thinks that advertising of that character should be revived, very good; and the veteran papers would be the ones to use. But I certainly do know that to utilise advertising space at the public expense for the character of advertisement I saw is wrong, no matter who is responsible for it. I take the minister's word that he is not.

I rise to add my word of commendation to what was said by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail). I have been keeping close watch on the operations of the soldier land settlement scheme ever since its inception and I can heartily commend the working out of the operations of the board so far as I have observed them. I do not view this matter from the political standpoint at all, nor from the standpoint of those who originated the scheme; nor am I looking at it from the point of view of those who are at present carrying it on. I am speaking entirely from the standpoint of the observer who has been watching it closely, and I can speak particularly of the work done in my own district of Prince Albert in Saskatchewan. I have visited these men in



Supply-Soldiers' Settlement
their homes, and have been in all corners of that district where they are established. I might give a few figures I have compiled in reference to the men who have been established there and also show the extent to which salvages have occurred. In that district 2,335 applications were made to the qualification board. Of this number 1,800 were passed as qualified, or practically 77 per cent. Some of those disqualified have gone into training; that is to say, they are working for fanners in the district with the intention, which will no doubt be afterwards carried out, of again coming under the qualification board and being passed and established on the land. There have been established some 1,509 soldier settlers, of which number 136 or 8 per cent have since been salvaged. That percentage is very small indeed as compared with the number of failures which may have occurred with the original homesteaders, men who went on the land and tried to establish themselves independently, and long before the organization of the Soldiers' Settlement Board. On the first of October last there were 1,281 with payments due. Of these 624 have since met their payments in full. I think that is a very good showing. Three hundred have made them in part. In spite of the fact that last year not very much money was made on the farms, indeed a great many farmers who were thoroughly established previously went behind, we find that these men under proper supervision have done particularly well. The applications in hand for the present year show that at least 150 new settlers will be established in this district. I would point out that this is entirely independent of the number who may be brought over from the British Isles by Major Ashton. These one hundred and fifty men made application on the spot and are likely to be established. The payments this year stand at 55.1 per cent of the amounts due; but there have also been pre-payments made that is to say payments not yet due, sufficient to bring that percentage up to 61.8 per cent. Considering these figures, and remembering what I have seen of the supervision exercised by the inspectors, as I said before, I wish to add my word of commendation. The project is working out particularly satisfactory, and I think it should get every assistance that we can give it.

I should like to call the minister's attention to one point in regard to the soldier land settlement scheme. Many of the soldiers when they returned already possessed land, but in order to get re-established they made application to the Soldiers' Settlement Board for loans to buy stock and imple-

ments. I understand that the board took security for these loans on practically everything the soldiers had, irrespective of the amount advanced. In many cases this has placed the borrowers in the unfortunate position of not being able to do business with their local stores, implement dealers and banks.
I have come across a few cases where the amount of security is out of all proportion to the amount loaned. I agree that the board should get adequate security for repayment of the loans made, but thus protected I think the board should be content and should release the balance of the security in order that the soldier settlers concerned can do business along the ordinary lines usual in farming communities. Having all their security tied up with the board these men cannot function as they should.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The reason for the delay in replying to the hon. gentleman's question in respect to taxation is that I wanted to be sure of my ground with regard not only to municipalities in his province but elsewhere. The Justice department has advised me to the effect that where lands are held by the Crown parliament has no authority to pay or guarantee taxes to the municipalities, crown lands being immune from taxation. So the matter would require readjustment and I am so informing the municipal authorities who have written me in connection with it. This government has no control over the collection of taxes from the man who is on the land, and can do nothing towards assisting him in their payment. I am speaking more
10 p.m. particularly of lands salvaged and returned to the control of the Dominion government. I admit frankly that it is a hardship, and I sought for some way to assist the municipalities, but that is the answer I have received, and I am giving it to the committee in order that hon. members may convey it to the parties interested.
With respect to my hon. friend's suggestion that we might abandon inspection, I must say that I do not agree with him, and I so stated at the beginning of my remarks this evening. I believe the success of this undertaking depends largely upon the inspection that is exercised over our soldier settlers. I do not mean to say that it should be of a kind that would be arduous upon the settler, but I do think that- this inspection and advice that is given to the settler when the inspector visits him is a feature that can be commended. I did not know until informed by my hon. friend that they were there every morning when the hens laid. That is news to me. However, if such is the case, it only speaks more highly of the very efficient manner in which these men are doing their duty.
It speaks well for the hens too.

I would like to say just a word about the way in which the soldier settlement scheme is working out in . my part of the country and in some other parts with which I am perhaps somewhat familiar. For some time I have taken a good deal of interest in the working of this board, and I have had an opportunity of meeting a good many returned men who are working under the provisions of the act. I know, and no one who comes from our part of the country but must know, that conditions among the soldier settlers are very hard in those parts, but I am not attributing that to the regulations of the Soldiers' Settlement Board or to the act under which they are working, or to the method under which the act is earned out. The condition of the soldier settler to my mind reflects the condition of agriculture as a whole in that part of the country, and if the conditions of agriculture as a whole are bad, as they are. the condition of the soldier settler will be bad also. But that can hardly be laid at the door of the board or of the scheme itself. I think that differentiation ought to be made. My own impression is that on the whole the soldier settlers are doing remarkably well considering all the circumstances. [DOT] We have to remember this, even when we compare them with other farmers who are in debt, that the soldier settler is more heavily indebted than the average civilian farmer. He has the advantage of better terms,'lower rates of interest, but on the other hand he owes practically 100 per cent, and in some cases over, of the value of his property. So he has a larger percentage of debt as a rule.	.
I was gratified to some extent to see that the percentage of collections had risen during the past year. I expected that of course due to the fact as has been stated that the total amount called for was much smaller, but what was much more significant was the fact that the actual amount realized was greater than last year. To my mind that carries far more significance than the percentage itself. How was that done? I do not believe it was done because the men themselves were making more money, because I do not believe they were. They could not make any more money than the farmers around them made during the last year. But I do believe this. It was due in part at least to the greater heart and the better spirit with which a great many of these men went at their work after some of the amendments that were made to the act last year. I am not speaking for political purposes at all. As a matter of fact, I have
Supply-Soldiers' Settlement

read a number of letters similar to the one mentioned by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, which did not attribute the entire credit to the Liberal government, but the fact remains that the effect of these amendments was somewhat belittled, I think, in saying that it was just a slight grant from the Treasury Board. It did not really take the form of a grant at all. What was done as far as the relinquishment of money was concerned was the cancellation of some $12,000,000 of interest due in the next four years. It was not money paid out by the Treasury Board as a grant, but money coming to the board by way of interest which was cancelled. That is something different from a grant. But more than that, I believe that a different principle was established in the loaning of money. We found, and I think any hon. member who followed the work last year and from his own experience at home knows that the'principle of having the heavier payments come due during the first years of a man's settlement, due to the short term for live stock and the long term for the land, was not a safe principle, and in my opinion not a right principle, because it is in the first years that a man finds it most difficult to make his payments. Parliament therefore tried to establish the principle of making the easy payments come first and the harder ones towards the end, when the settler would be more properly settled on the land.
I simply rose to mention these two points. One was to explain a little more closely what had been done, and the second was to draw that distinction between the conditions under which all agriculture was suffering and the conditions which were due to the Soldiers' Settlement Board itself. I can say in all fairness, as a somewhat disinterested though not uninterested observer, that I believed the act is working out fairly well, that the work is carried on fairly efficiently by the men employed, and that on the whole a very fair spirit exists among the returned soldier settlers towards the board under which they work and the officials with whom they come in contact.

I do not want to be misunderstood. Like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, it was the working of the board of which I was speaking, and not of the wisdom of' the act itself. I believe it is much too soon to say whether the land settlement scheme for soldiers has proved to be a success or not. It may prove to be; it may not. This is true. It came at a time when it was exceedingly hard for people

going on the land. I notice in many of the letters I have received that the men who have made the fewest payments are the most optimistic about the scheme and those who have paid the most are the most pessimistic. That struck as being an odd thing. But we should give praise where praise is due, and I think that the Soldiers' Settlement Board, taking them in the large, have been very kind and considerate, and those who went to visit the soldiers on the land must have done so in a humane and kindly way since the expression of opinion regarding them is so unanimous.
I rise to ask the minister if it would be possible to have the settlers in Ontario, for instance, make their payments in the spring instead of in the fall. In grain growing provinces, such as in the middle West, to pay all debts in the fall when the grain is to be sold works out very nicely, but not in' Ontario where in the fall there is very little to sell. Besides that, there are debts coming due which would take what little the soldier settlers have to sell. Possibly a couple of hundred -who answered me asked for that change to be made; at least, they said it would mean a great deal to them if they could pay their debts in the spring instead of in the fall, because under the present method they were forced to sell their grain which they wanted to feed. I do not know whether it would be possible for the minister to make the change. I know it is difficult to have one method apply in one province and another in another province, but they do ask me to express that wish for them.

Grant to H. H. Moss, to cover expenses in connectior with his illegal arrest, $595.58.

Will the minister explain

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have here
a written explanation of the matter. There was one Harold Moss, whom the department were seeking to prosecute. He went to the United States and an arrest was made, but unfortunately we arrested the wrong man, with the result that there was a protest from Washington from the Secretary of State, who suggested that the government of Canada make a compensation to one Moss, an American citizen who was arrested instead of the man we were after:
A letter was received by His Majesty's Embassy at Washington from the United States Secretary of State, suggesting that the government of Canada make compensation to one Harry Moss, an employee of the National Board of Fire Underwriters of New York City, who was wrongfully arrested in Chicago on the 3rd November, 1921, at the direction of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, on being erroneously identified with Harold H. Moss, who was wanted on charges of false pretences and fraud in connection with transactions with the Soldier Settlement Board.
From the board's records, it is clear that one Harry Moss of Chicago was improperly arrested on an in-fomation laid and warants secured by the board for the arrest of Harold H. Moss, formerly of Winnipeg. The Board is not in a position to say what injury Harry Moss suffered by reason of the improper arrest.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
nor if injury was suffered, is it in a position to say what compensation should be paid, or how the matter should be disposed of. It would appear to the board that the entire matter is one involving the administration of justice, and must be determined by the opinion and recommendation of the Justice department.
Should it be determined by the Justice department that compensation should be paid by the Canadian authorities, it will be necessary to determine on which department the responsibility rests for the improper arrest, and the board on that ground does not accept the responsibility.
In order that full information may be available for the proper consideration of the legal and international questions involved, a brief history of the case as it appears in the board's records, is given herewith.
As a result of certain information placed before the parliamentary committee on Re-establishment, the board instituted an enquiry under Section 55 of the Soldier Settlement Act, into certain land purchases in the province of Manitoba. At this enquiry, taken under oath, it transpired that in 1919 one H. H. Moss of Winnipeg had sold to the board certain farms, and the evidence thus taken established, in the opinion of C. H. Locke, legal counsel employed, a prima facie case against the said H. H. Moss of perjury, obtaining money by false pretences, and other criminal wrongdoing. Moss was a witness in the early stages of the enquiry. On the advice of counsel the board placed the facts before the Attorney General's department of Manitoba, and in consultation with the Deputy Attorney General of Manitoba, laid certain informations against H. H. Moss and had warrants for his arrest issued. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police had been employed to assist in gathering evidence for the enquiry, and the warrant for arrest was placed in their hands. On attempting to execute same, it was ascertained that H. H. Moss had fled from justice, and was somewhere in the United States.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police pursued their attempts to* locate H. H. Moss in the United States, and their agents finally reported that he had been located in Chicago, and they asked the board to undertake to defray the expense of their sending a police constable to Chicago to verify the reports of the police agents. The board agreed to do this, and constable Downey was sent from Winnipeg to Chicago by the R.C.M.P. authorities. The board supplied the R.C. M.P. with a good photograph of the accused and with a full description and other means of identification. Constable Downey reported that he had definitely located the accused in the offices of the National Board of Fire Underwriters in Chicago; that he had personally seen the accused; and that there was no doubt of his identity. On the advice of counsel, the board submitted the facts to the Department of Justice, and obtained authority to commence extradition proceedings, and the R.C.M.P. were therefore authorized to make the arrest. This was done and Mr. Locke having acted as counsel at the board's enquiry and being conversant with all the facts, was sent to Chicago to direct the proceedings. On his arrival he immediately discovered that the man arrested was not H. H. Moss, the accused, and consequently ordered his release. The whereabouts of Harold H. Moss, the accused, have not since been discovered.
We are asking for this sum because we believe we shall be liable for the wrongful arrest of the American citizen Moss, who was not the man we were after.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: This is accounted for partly by requisitions and partly by transfers and some increases of the .staff. There have been transferred to the permanent those who were on the temporary list. Under the act of 1918 the statistical work of all the various departments of government was transferred to the Bureau of Statistics. So we have transferred some of these employees from other departments, and to carry on the work it is necessary to make these employees permanent in accordance with the requirements of the Civil Service Commission.

What strikes one at first glance is the very substantial increase in the number of employees in this department. An increase in a single year from 300 to 345 employees is rather staggering, while the increase in the cost of administration as a result of this increase in staff is from $425,000 to $476,000. What was the necessity for this enormous increase in the staff?

As I have just explained, it does not necessarily mean that there is this enormous increase in the staff nor in the



Supply-Trade and Commerce
cost of administration. Under the system of book-keeping, to meet the requirements of the auditor general moneys must be voted either for temporary or for permanent employees. The Civil Service Commission refuses any longer to grant certificates for the temporary employees who have been in this department for a number of years, and this necessitates their being made permanent. As a matter of fact I think the increase in staff is warranted in view of the statistical information demanded. My hon. friend will observe that 37 of these 45 additional employees are in the Bureau of Statistics. There are only two additional employees in the administration branch of the department, and under readjustment during the year these will disappear. The other six are in the commercial intelligence bureau.
Were they not all in the department last year?

Some have been transferred from the Department of Labour, some from the Interior department, and some were on the temporary list and had been there for a number of years. If we had a system of book-keeping whereby we could have a lump sum to run each department during the year it would not be necessary to vote so much, but when we have to provide for those who are now temporary employees and will be transferred and made permanent after this vote is passed, my hon. friend can see the necessity for putting through these different votes.

Turning to page 66 of the Main Estimates, where the various activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce are set out, it will be found that for the carrying on of that department last year we voted $3,252,000. This year all the minister asks is $3,029,000. He proposes a reduction of $222,000 in round figures. No new services are enumerated on page 66, apparently no greater activities are contemplated over last year, if anything the work of the department will be decreased this year because about a quarter of a million dollars less is asked for in the Main Estimates. Notwithstanding that, on turning to civil government we find this increase of 45 in the number of employees and something like $50,000 in salaries. You can go over all the details of civil government and though we are year by year getting farther from war activities, when so large a Civil Service was necessary, it is strange that the cost of civil government seems to increase. This year there is an increase of $252,000. This is one

of the departments of civil government. If we may judge by the Main Estimates its activities will be less even than they were last year. But whatever we may provide in the estimates, for some reason or other the cost of the staff of the department goes up, and as a result we are asked to provide by taxation a quarter of a million dollars more than we did last year. It is all very well for my hon. friend to say that these clerks have been transferred from some other departments, but those other departments do not show a decrease, and the Main Estimates show that the amount in excess of last year for civil government is just a shade over a quarter of a million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as my hon. friend has referred to all departments of civil government, and he has confined himself to a study of the civil government estimates, I think you will agree with me that it is not the proper manner in which to examine the expenditure for administration so far as salaries are concerned. Take the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, almost all the employees are temporary and do not figure at all in the civil government list. There is this year in the estimates for salaries for the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment department a reduction of $1,000,000. Now, my hon. friend I know wants to be fair. He says there is an increase in the civil government expenditure of a quarter of a million dollars. I grant that it may be so, but even if it is, if there is a reduction of salaries in my department of $1,000,000, there will be a saving of three-quarters of a million dollars this year in salaries. My hon. friend will admit that-yes, he has to admit that.
That is as to temporary employees. I am talking of those on the permanent list.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My *hon. friend says these are temporary employees. What did he mean when he referred to the war? He said the farther we get away from the war the more we pay in salaries. The Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment department is a war department if it is anything at all. There was a reduction last year of $1,000,000 in salaries. This year there is a similar reduction. My hon. friend fails to take that into account, but he should do so if he wants to be fair.
That is a different proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
No, it is not a different proposition at all. My hon. friend intimates that there is an increase in the amount for salaries for administration while there should

Supply-Trade and Commerce
be a decrease because we are getting farther away from thfe war. I agree with
10 p.m. him. But when, he confines his remarks to civil government he becomes-unwittingly I am sure-unfair and states the position wrongly, and I think he will admit it because he wants to be fair. This is for the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment department-a reduction of $1,000,000. What about the Defence department? I think 1,600 temporary employees have been dispensed with there. That does not appear in the civil government estimates. There is also probably over a million dollars of reduction in salaries paid. My hon. friend says it seems that the expenditure is increasing all the time. No, it is decreasing every year, and by large amounts. The cost of civil government, no doubt, remains much about the same in almost every department, and it will remain about the same no matter what government is in power. I rose mainly for the purpose of pointing out that it is very unfair to confine one's observations to the civil government estimates; it is absolutely unfair because really there is a decrease of over $2,000,000 in salaries paid by this government this year for employees all over the country.

This item that we are discussing now is the civil government vote. It has nothing to do with the temporary employees which the various departments of the government employ and have employed since the war. It was not only in the war departments, such as the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and the Department of Militia and Defence, that temporary clerks were taken on. Why, they were almost innumerable in the Finance department and in every other department of the government owing to the war. But this vote we are discussing now, and in regard to which I charge there is an increase when there should be no increase, is a permanent vote. There is no cutting down in this vote. These men are simply appointed to the permanent staff and there will be more of them there again next year and the year after that again. Instead of decreasing the cost of civil government this government is increasing it. I am aware that there is a vanishing expenditure, or should be, in my hon. friend's Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. I know that in one year or a year and a half we let out from the Militia department 8,000 temporary employees. I should think we are within reasonable distance now of closing up the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-e'stab-lishment altogether; but the fact that we
have let many hundreds of war employees go who are no longer necessary, is that a justification for increasing the permanent staff that governs this country? That is my point, and the only point I wish to make. Instead of retrenchment we have increase. The times do not justify increase; the activities of the government do not justify increase; the business of the country being done to-day does not, justify this increase. The fact is the civil service of Canada is being loaded up in this way with permanent employees, and you cannot dispense with them as you can with temporary employees by simply telling them to go. They obtain a fixed place in the service of Canada. Next year I am willing to predict there will be no decrease in this particular vote, but that the cost of civil government in Canada will be more than it is this year.

My hon. friend knows that under civil government we have employees classed as temporary as well as those on the permanent list. There are in all departments many employees who have been on the: temporary^ list for years, and the Civil Service Commission have ruled that they should be put on the permanent list. I think it is only reasonable when a man has been in a department five, ten or fifteen years and it is evident that his services are required that he should be put on the permanent list. You have to pay him anyway.
My hon. friend, on the other hand, referred to a reduction of $222,000, and he takes that as an indication that we propose less activity during the year. That is not true. We anticipate greater activity during the year. I can show my hon. friend where these reductions were made. In the first place there is the census staff, which my hon. friend knows is taken on every ten years. Those are temporary employees. There is a reduction of $115,000 there.
That will not appear in this vote, will it?

No, but it was in connection with this vote that my hon. friend anticipated less activity during the year. Then $85,000 was spent for improvements to the elevator at Vancouver. The department had nothing whatever to do with that. It was all handled by the Board of Grain Commissioners. We are also making a reduction of $10,000 in the Commercial Intelligence department, travelling and miscellaneous expenses in connection with the junior trade commissioners. There is a reduction of $15,000 for exhibitions and publicity; a reduction of $5,900 in the Weights
Supply-Trade and Commerce

and Measures branch; $6,330 in the Gas and Electricity branch; and $50,000 through printing now being done elsewhere. This does not in any way affect civil government, and no person knows it better than my hon friend, who has been in charge of a department himself and has had considerable experience in parliament.

It strikes me that the reductions in all the services my hon. friend has just enumerated must mean less work than there was to do formerly with a larger expenditure. When the expenditure was greater and there was more work to do, more clerical assistance would of necessity be required- more men to do the work. I think it is quite clear from these estimates that there is going to be a considerable reduction in the work of the department. Then why add forty or fifty to the staff of a department to do less work? Let me put to my hon. friend the case of a business man doing a business this year entailing an expenditure of $3,000,000. He has his staff and does the work satisfactorily with the number he has. Next year he is going to do a business of $2,500,000. Do you think he is going to add fifty clerks to his staff to do a less amount of business? It strikes me as too obvious for argument that with a smaller expenditure and less departmental activity, the department should get along at least with the same staff it had last year. Does not that seem reasonable? Instead of that the minister proposes a large increase in the staff and an additional expenditure of $50,000 to pay for it. It may be that he has been loaded down in his department with other services he did not have last year, but I doubt very much if there is any saving shown in these other departments from which his additional staff has come. I have not looked into the estimates and I cannot say as to that, but my experience of nearly thirty years in this House has been that the cost of civil government has gone up under every government. I do not believe there ever was a time when the need for retrenchment was as great as it is to-day, and surely it is not a matter for censure that one should point out this substantial increase which the government proposes for the coming year when we cannot afford the money, when every dollar of the increase has to be met by taxation of the people. What I protest against not only in the Department of Trade and Commerce but in all the departments of the government is that the temporary staffs are being carried on. The war staffs are certainly being reduced from year to year, but the temporary staffs of the

department still exist and they are paid out of special votes in the case of almost every department. They have them there and year by year they get them wedged in as permanents, whether by the aid of the Civil Service Commission or in defiance of that body I cannot say, but the result is seen in the estimates brought down to the House. There is an aggregate increase of-I said $250,000- but it is an increase of $265,000, in the cost of the clerical work, practically, of the government of Canada.
Would the minister tell us how many temporary employees in the department have been placed on the permanent staff?
They have not been put in yet. We cannot put them in until this vote goes through.
What are the details?
The statutory increases amount to $16,000, and there are 45 to be transferred.
From temporary to permanent positions?
Yes; some of them are transferred from other departments.

I notice that the minister mentioned the Department of Labour. I looked up the appropriations for that department and I found there had been a decrease in the staff of about 27; that is about 20 less than the increase in the department. I should like to say just one word about the Statistical branch. It is now, and has been for some years-two or three years I think-entirely in the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Since 1918-no, prior to that. In 1918 there was an act passed transferring the statistics of every department to the Dominion bureau.

I do not recollect the exact date but I knew it was back about that time. I simply wish to say this: The Bureau of Statistics, since that unity has been brought about, is a department which is of great use, not only to the members of this House but to the people of the country in general. I remember that when I came into this House first, about 1917, if you wished to obtain any statistics regarding minerals, for example, or grain, or any other department of government, you would ring up the department, perhaps the Department of the Interior, the Department of Agriculture, or some other department. You would probably be referred from the one to the other and from the other back

Supply-Trade and Commerce
to the one. I remember on one occasion being referred by telephone to seven or eight different offices when I tried to get certain details. At the present time one can ring up or write to the Bureau of Statistics and get-on most occasions, and on most subjects concerned with government-the figures or statistics which one desires, and I have yet to see them pointed out as given in a mistaken way. I just wished to put myself on record as expressing on my own behalf alone, but I am sure it is the opinion of many in this House, an appreciation of the work that is being done by the Bureau of Statistics under Mr. Coats. I believe that once in a while-in the Civil Service as in other branches of life-a few words of commendation where they are well deserved, as they certainly are in the case of the Bureau of Statistics, are decidely in place.
I would like to ask the minister how many of the forty-five employees referred to have been transferred from the Department of Labour?
Nine.
From what departments were they transferred?

I could not give that information. I should say that nine is the total number that were transferred. I think most of them came from the Labour department, but some of them may have been transferred from the Forestry branch.
I notice a reference to "office appliance operators". What work do these employees do?
They are the men who run the multigraph machines in the Statistical department and other branches.
Item agreed to.
May I ask the minister what other items in the Department of Trade and Commerce remain to be dealt with? Has he nearly finished the estimates of that department?
No, there are some steamship subsidies yet to be dealt with.

I would like to point out that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), as the minister knows, having been formerly Minister of Trade and Commerce, usually looks after those estimates in the interest of hon. members on this side. The hon. gentleman is not in the chamber to-night, unfortunately he is engaged elsewhere, and I would like to have these items
held over. I would prefer if the minister would do that until the hon. member is able to be present I do not know that there is any special matter that he wishes to take up, but I should like the minister to hold these votes over for the time being.

I would like to get them
cleaned up but I will say this: I did defer other estimates to suit the former Minister of Trade and Commerce, my immediate predecessor, and it is quite likely there will be some small items in the supplementaries. I will allow the hon. member for Vancouver Centre wide discussion on those.
If the minister agrees that on some other item we may come back to these particular appropriations, if we wish for further details, I think as far as we are concerned we will be satisfied.

Anything you wish.
Patent and Copyright-salaries, $175,865; contingencies, $35,000.
There is no change in the number of employees, but there is a slight-increase in the amount for salaries owing entirely to reclassification.

Item agreed to.
Canada Grain Act-additional amount required, $200,000.
I should like to suggest to the minister that this is a large item to be taken at this late hour, and that as there is likely to be some discussion it had better be left over.

I do not object strenuously to letting it stand but I will explain this: The Board of Grain Commissioners estimated the amount required last year at $1,342,869. It was reduced in the department some $42,000. There were some accrued payments for the previous year, 1921-22, amounting to $50,000 and there were certain increases of salary endorsed by the commissioners. Furthermore we had an additional expenditure owing to having to handle last year almost the largest crop in our history. That explains the increased . amount required. The elevators administered by the Board of Grain Commissioners are a paying and not a losing proposition, and this is the estimate which has been prepared by the board and sent down to us.

What effect
would the possible establishment of a wheat board have on this matter?

None whatever. We would administer this act just the same.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
There have been some changes in the personnel of the grain commission. Would the minister tell the House what changes have been made and what appointments have been made since last year?

The Board of Grain Commissioners are appointed for a period of ten years. The term of Mr. Staples, one of the commissioners, expired last year, and the government appointed in his place Mr. Mat Snow, a well-known western gentleman. Then Mr. Jones resigned voluntarily. His time was up this year, and, incidentally, I want to pay a tribute to Mr. Jones whom I regarded as a man who thoroughly understood the grain business, but he voluntarily retired and the government appointed to replace him Mr. Robinson, who had been associated for *: number of years with the Saskatchewan CoOperative Elevator Company. Mr. Hether-ington is now replacing Mr. Jones as general manager. Previous to that one of the commissioners, Mr. Jones, was manager of the system. ' Mr. Hetherington, who had been for many yeara secretary, is now general manager. I am not sure who succeeded Mr. Hetherington as secretary. It was on the recommendation of the commissioners, and Mr. Leslie Boyd still remains the chairman.
Any present indication of making any more changes?
Not the least whatever.

I am very well acquainted with Mr. Jones, and I agree with the minister that his retirement is a great loss to the board because he is a very able man. I wish to ask the minister a question in regard to the different elevators that the Board of Grain Commissioners are handling for his department. There is one at Port Arthur and one, I think, at Saskatoon. Will he give us the details as to where they are and the business done at the present time?
M. ROBB: I have not the records before me as to the details of the business they are doing. In addition to those mentioned by my hon. friend, there is an internal terminal elevator at Moose Jaw, one in Saskatoon, and there are also elevators at Vancouver and at Calgary. The elevator at Vancouver has been putting through a lot of grain this season. Indeed, last year we put more grain through that elevator in Vancouver than during all the years since its construction, and this year I think we will put through more than twice as much as we put through last year. We were operating it 
and using the Calgary elevator as a reservoir, so that when the superintendent at Vancouver was able to see by the ships coming in, that he was going to empty his elevator in Vancouver, word would be sent down to Calgary to send on the reserves that were there, and in that way we have been able to handle the crop with satisfaction.

In most of the elevators, except the Vancouver elevator, and I think the Port Arthur elevator, there has been a decrease.
Yes, last year.
With the large crop from the prairie provinces, why was there a decrease ?

The minister informed the House that this propostiion was self-sustaining. Can he tell us the revenue and to what account the money went?
Would the hon. member like to go back several years?
No, just two years.

In 1921-22 the revenue was $1,937,325.02 and the expenditure $1,235,000, leaving a surplus of $702,325.02. In 1922-23, up to February 28th-that is part of this year's crop, the revenue was $2,080,348.75 and the expenditure $1,231,667.80 leaving a surplus $1,848,680.95.
