Yes.

From a rumour circulating some few years ago, which seemed to me to be very well founded, it appeared to me the department might suffer a loss in regard to a carload of grain shipped to the United States, passing out of the mixing elevator. The purchaser in the United States refused to receive

Supply-Trade and Commerce
the grain on the ground that it was not up to grade. The department had it inspected at Buffalo, and I believe by the order of the grain commissioners it was stored at Buffalo, and the new sample being graded by the inspector, he found the grade No. 3 and 4 tough, where the cargo was in fact graded out at No. 3. I understood the ground taken by the mixing elevator was that they had received from the government a regular certificate, and that they were therefore, not liable for any loss because the grain was not up to the mark. The purchaser took the stand that he would not accept it, and I understood there was some good reason to believe the loss might possibly fall on the department. Could the minister give us any information as to whether that matter is settled or how it stands?

No, there has been no record of any claim coming in to the government. My recollection is that the matter was adjusted. I am glad my hon. friend has mentioned that, because it did not occur to me when I was answering some other questions. This complaint of a shipment of grain going out from Fort William to Buffalo was brought to my attention some time last summer. I ordered an investigation, and as a result of that, I instructed the commissioners to fire two of the employees who were grain inspectors and who, we had reason to believe, had, to' say the least, neglected their duties. This had a wholesome effect on the others. I have heard of no complaint since then.

I am glad to hear that. I do not know whether the minister will have this information or not. Some years ago there was a heavy loss owing to the difference in weights between the elevator at Fort William and the transfer elevators at Owen Sound, Collingwood and other places, of about 50,000 bushels a year. Changes were put into effect in 1908 which remedied that matter, and for a year or two conditions were all right. I was wondering whether that remedy has been effective up to the present time or not. Can the minister state whether there is any discrepancy or not in the weights of grain shipments as they arrive at Owen Sound, Collingwood, Port Elgin and, in fact, Buffalo as well?

There are very few complaints coming to the department now as regards either inspection or weight. We recently had some complaints from overseas regarding the weight of a cargo of grain shipped out of Montreal- We are going to send a couple of men over there. We will send one man from
the inspection department, and I think the Montreal Harbour Commissioners are going to send a man to look into this. We want to satisfy our customers on the other side that we in Canada have every desire to see that business is done right, upon a fair basis. As my hon. friend knows, the grain is weighed out in this country in large draughts; on the other side it is weighed in smaller draughts. Then there is a question as to what may have happened to some of this cargo in transit. The boat may have sprung a leak. There may have been some wet grain in the bottom, dumped over. We are going to look into this matter in an endeavour to satisfy the claim on the other side.
Are there any elevators in Ontario under the control of the department?
No. The grain commissioners have a certain supervision over these elevators; but we do not own any in Ontario.
There is one at Port Colborne.
That is under the Railway department.
Has the department not been requested by some interests in Ontario to establish an elevator?
We have from time to time such requests from all parts of the country, where people imagine an elevator would be a very nice proposition.
Within the last year?
Yes, we had a request from Ontario.
What is the total value, roughly, of these elevators, including plant and equipment?

In my judgment, these elevators could mot be built to-day for their original cost. The capital cost of the Port Arthur house is $1,415,336.31; of the Saskatchewan elevator, $1,134,745.73; of the Moose Jaw elevator $1,322,725.50. Of the three houses I have cited, the capacity is 3,250,000 bushels, 3,500,000 bushels, and 3,500,000 bushels respectively. There is at Calgary a smaller house with a capacity of 2,500,000 bushels and costing $884,564.35. The house at Vancouver, with a capacity of 1,250,000 bushels, cost $837,351.71. The total capital investment is $5,594,723.60, for a capacity of 14,000,000 bushels.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The minister, I think, said that there was no write-off for depreciation for buildings or plant.
No.

If a proper depreciation were set up against this capital invested, and if the profits were only as stated by the minister, namely, as I recall, $700,000 one year, and $800,000 last year, this would mep that this business is not being very profitably carried on.

The accountant at Fort William has prepared a statement which has been sent here; but I cannot find any statement of interest, although he has an item of $294,000 under profit and loss, which might be attributed to interest. That shows a percentage of profit on the capital investment in plant in the Port Arthui house of almost 5-32 per cent.

As this is an elevator appropriation, the minister might tell the committee what has been done since last session regarding the promise made then by the minister in answer to a question asked on this side of the House as to a terminal elevator for central and western Ontario. A few years ago there waited upon the government a deputation consisting of representatives of, I might say, all the farming and business interests of central and western Ontario. I understand the policy in relation to elevators is that there shall be equality of treatment; that where a government elevator is erected in the West, an elevator shall be erected in Ontario. A memorandum was presented by a deputation of 200 people including the United Farmers of Ontario, the Grain Growers of the province, the late Lieutenant Governor Clarke of Ontario, Mr. Manning Doherty, the harbour commissioners of five or six very important harbours, representing that Ontario had been discriminated against as regards a terminal elevator to serve the farmers of that province. Ontario is suffering under a handicap in the matter of transportation. There are many flag stations where there are no elevators, and the United Farmers of Ontario and the harbour commissioner's of Toronto in a very elaborate memorial which I read last session, pointed out to the government the necessity of such a terminal elevator in central Ontario. This is very much needed from the farmer's standpoint, because he has no place to take his grain crop, and he loses a good deal of the price, his time and so forth. The need of such an elevator is, indeed, apparent to every-
body. Years ago, in my city there were a number of elevators on the water front, but now we have none. There is an elevator at Port Colborne and one at Fort William, and I agree with the minister that there is no need for another elevator for through-going crop. But this elevator is not for through crops going to the Old Country via Buffalo. The need in Ontario is a local one; the farmer needs some elevator where he can put his crop in the winter and leave it until such time as water-going traffic can take it to its proper destination. A return brought down to the House some time ago showed that there are a great many elevators in the West. Well, the people are not, objecting to that. Rather, they are encouraging the government to put up these elevators; and the minister since taking office has been active in many branches of his department. I commend him as far as this goes. But so far as Ontario is concerned I want to urge upon him the great necessity that exists for terminal elevators for the farmers of this province. The deputation that waited upon a former government was drawn from Peterborough, Stratford and from the whole northern division of the Grand Trunk, as well as from central and western Ontario. This large deputation waited upon Sir Thomas White, but the government' of that day could not see its way, owing to the war, to take practical action in the' matter. They admitted the necessity there was for an elevator of this description but they attributed their inability to do anything to the financial stress of the time. A hundred and twenty farmers' organizations petitioned the government, and I shall not read the memo to-night, because the minister has a copy of it. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) asked the minister last session to give this matter his consideration and the minister promised that during the recess he would look into it. The question was discussed the other day in the Ontario legislature, but it was found that that body could do nothing in the premises, because the matter was a federal one. Now, I may say that while the United Farmers of Ontario have no particular love for the city I come from, nevertheless they recommend that the elevator be established in Toronto. I am not asking at this moment that this recommendation be acted upon; all I ask is that an elevator be established somewhere in the province to meet the economic and transportation necessities of the farmers of Ontario. It is not so much the site of the elevator that matters; what is important is that one be established. We want a terminal elevator for the small farmer so that

Supply-Trade and Commerce
he may have somewhere to take his crop for the winter months, because as things stand at present he has no such facilities. 1 know that the minister is sympathetically disposed to this question and while I do not want to delay the committee on this item to-night, I hope that the minister will give us an assurance that he will take steps to meet the representations that have been made by the farmers of Ontario. I believe he will be waited upon by another deputation and I trust that he will give them a chance to put their case plainly before him. I think it is in the interests of the country that he should make a declaration of policy with regard to the desirability of establishing this terminal elevator on lake Ontario or lake Erie for central and western Ontario. This is an important matter and I sincerely trust that the minister will give it his most careful consideration.

While I am always glad to meet a deputation from Ontario and Toronto particularly, I think I would rather go up to Toronto and look into the matter there. I have been promising my hon. friend a long time to go there, and I think I can assure him now that before next session I will go to that city and look the thing over. I might point out that the way freights are arranged in this country, working west to east, there is considerable elevator capacity at Depot Harbour, Owen Sound, Midland, Goderich, Port Huron, Port Credit and Port Colborne. I am inclined to think there is need of more capacity at Port Colborne. I would point out to my hon. friend, however, that while there is considerable elevator capacity up there, perhaps not enough for their requirements, there are at Kingston two very large houses in addition to one at Prescott, which were practically idle during the last few years. However, I renew my promise to the hon. member to visit Toronto.

The minister, having had a conference with the Grain Commissioners in the last few weeks, said that some complaints were made during the year with regard to screenings. Possibly the point may have been raised in the course of the conference, and the minister may be able to give us information. The point I refer to is this. The farmers were in many cases paid very small amounts, sometimes even so low as 50 cents or $1 a ton for screenings of excellent quality. I am not referring to screenings that are so cheap to-day that they are thrown into the lake. I know there is a quantity of that class of screenings. I am referring, however, to valuable screenings; what I have in
mind particularly is white cleaned oats. This should have been worth $12 or $15 a ton, but the farmer received only $1 a ton for it. If that point arose during the conference perhaps the minister can give us some information in reference to it.
We discussed that, and the Board of Grain, Commissioners are now preparing for me a complete statement. I intend that that shall be one of the questions to be inquired into during the summer.

I was going to mention something about screenings myself when my hon. friend (Mr. Millar) brought up the point.
I was pleased to hear him refer to it because there has been a good deal of dissussion at the head of the lakes with reference to that question. As the minister knows, both the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) and myself have asked questions regarding the disposal of screenings because charges have been made that the screenings have not been turned back in the condition in which they should be. In the old days before the amendment to the Grain Act, the overages were mixed up with the question of screenings, and they are yet to a certain extent. But the main charge seems to be that instead of people getting back the screenings as they should really get them, in their original condition, they receive, as a matter of fact, refuse * screenings. I am not making a positive statement of fact, but this charge appears in the press occasionally, and one hears it on the street too; and sometimes as a member of the constituency I get letters in reference to the question. It is stated that when anyone asks for screenings he simply gets refuse screenings, instead of the original screenings which are worth a great deal more. The matter is very much as the hon. member has stated. I asked some questions of the minister, by correspondence and on the order paper, regarding this matter with a view to obtaining further information. At present the question seems to be in a rather hazy state. I do not say that as a criticism of the Board of Grain Commissioners, because I believe they are an able body who are trying to carry out their duties as well as they can. But in the past , the question of screenings and dockage has been allowed to drift along, and now there seems to be coming from the prairie provinces, as well as from some dealers at the head of the lakes, who wish to buy screenings, the charge that they cannot get what they are entitled to receive. I would suggest to the minister therefore that it would be a good idea to have the whole question thoroughly investigated. I might mention a concrete

Supply-Trade and Commerce
circumstance in reference to this matter. A man named Harvey from one of the prairie provinces came to the head of the lakes about a year and a half ago bringing in unfinished sheep which he fed there on screenings. He brought them in very ordinary selling condition and he fed them during the winter on screenings he obtained almost for nothing, because the refuse screenings at that time were really used for fuel in a number of the business blocks of the city. I have forgotten how many sheep he had, but I think the number was around 10,000; and he fed them on the refuse screenings which he got practically for a song. He sold those sheep in the spring very much fattened and in excellent shape for market, and he made a very profitable deal in the transaction. This winter he has increased the number of the sheep he is feeding there, and although I cannot give the exact figure, I think it is around 20,000. This winter, although he has had to pay a higher price for these refuse screenings, he is fattening a large number of sheep in the same way as he did last winter. So it shows the possibilities for the future from the live stock standpoint, which is probably one of the most important branches of agriculture not only in my section of the country-in which naturally I am interested-but throughout the whole Dominion. Formerly these refuse screenings were of no value to the elevator people and were taken out and dumped into the lake. According to replies given by the minister to questions placed on the order paper, and to letters written by myself, the Board of Grain Commissioners claim that the elevator companies have been losing money in handling these screenings. Then it is claimed in rebuttal by one of the dealers at the head of the lakes in letters to me and to other members in this House-at least I assume so from some of the questions put on the order paper-that if he could get these screenings at a fair price he could make a very fine stock feed out of them. And the fact that last winter so many sheep were fattened simply on the refuse screenings shows that they contain very good feed for stock.

Could the hon. gentleman tell us whether the owners of those sheep sustained any loss by reason of some of their stock being attacked by disease, said to be due to their being fed on these screenings?

No. I know the gentleman quite well and his first lot were a great success. I believe this winter-I have only a hazy recollection of it-some disease did develop, but it had nothing to do with the feeding. The
TMr. Manion.]
first winter he fattened ten thousand sheep very successfully with very little shelter-[DOT] only an old plant which had been built for another purpose; but this winter I am not sure that he has any shelter at all for his sheep, and the last I heard they promised to be as successful a lot as he fattened the previous winter. It was a very unexpected result, and if my hon. friends on my left do not know about it I imagine they will be more interested in the success of the experiment than any other hon. members. Mr. Harvey is the gentleman who has made such a success in the use of these screenings for the fattening of sheep. Therefore, this whole question of screenings might very well be thoroughly looked into not only from the standpoint of the fattening of sheep, but in relation to stock feeding generally. I might add that I have been told someone is going to bring in a number of cattle next winter to fatten on these refuse screenings and counts on having the same success as Mr. Harvey has had with sheep. But there is also the phase of the question which my hon. friends to the left have brought up on several occasions this session, namely, that the grain trade was not treating the wheat growers fairly. The remarks of my hon, friend who has just sat down (Mr. Millar) show that he at least is thinking of that phase. From what I have read in the press many farmers feel that they have not been able to get back, even from the government elevators at Saskatoon and other points, the screenings to which they are entitled. I read an article recently in a newspaper in which a farmer stated that he had shipped a car of wheat from one of the prairie provinces to Vancouver, and that by the time the car reached Vancouver he had lost money on the shipment owing to the freight he had to pay on the dockage. He claimed-and he is supported by others-that if he had got back what was coming to him-I do not say this positively for I am not a grain man, but I have heard it said at different times by experienced grain men-that if he had got back the broken wheat and various other grains and seeds in the screenings of value as feed he would have been in a position to gain very markedly on his shipment. I only refer to that in passing. My hon. friends to my left probably are very much more familiar with the question than I am and will be able to judge as to the correctness of the claim, but I know it has been very much discussed among grain men at the head of the lakes.
I repeat, I think the minister would do well to have the whole question investigated, because I do not think it is the policy of those

Supply-Trade and Commerce
in charge of the government elevators to treat the farmers of the West unfairly. Certainly those elevators were not only built for the convenience of the western farmers, but also for another purpose-that of acting as a check upon the privately owned elevators. In the past at least there have been vast amounts of overages which were very, very valuable in nearly all the elevators, including those operated by the government. So the minister has within his power an opportunity, through the Board of Grain Commissioners-and I am sure he will be glad to take advantage of it- to look into this whole question and see that justice is done. That is all I am asking. I have no interest whatever in any shape, manner or form in the grain business except as a citizen of this country, but I am slightly familiar with it as a resident at the head of the lakes where we have such immense elevator capacity.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Pardon me, Mr. Chairman, no. The minister was to give us an answer.

May I repeat again that it will be a subject for inquiry. Already the Board of Grain Commissioners have suggested to Mr. Clark of the Department of Agriculture, who has charge of the administration of the Stock Feeds Act, that he should go up to Fort William and ascertain the real value of these screenings.

I wish the minister would be good enough to refer the observations made by my hon. friend for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and those I am about to make now to whatever body is going to consider this matter. The crux of the screenings problem was I think brought up in a question asked a few weeks ago by one of the members from Manitoba-I have forgotten his riding. It is so difficult sometimes to approach a question of this kind without appearing to be more or less viciously attacking the
11 p.m. elevator interests, and therefore I should like to make it perfectly clear that that is not my object at the moment. There is a statement of fact, however, which I desire to make, and I am sure it cannot be gainsaid. It is this, that when a car of wheat is first cleaned dockage is made because of the presence of a certain percentage of dirt-chaff, seeds and so forth. In that first dockage there is a large proportion of broken wheat, oats, buckwheat, flaxseed and purposes. That belongs rightly to the other grains that are very valuable for feed farmer, and he should get full value for it.
That fact, I think, is admitted, and this is what I want my hon. friends to my left to get as well: That it is not the screenings that are sold at $1.50 a ton that was referred to the other day. The screenings sold for $1.50 a ton is the residue after this first screenings has been put through a second process and all the valuable wheat, oats, buckwheat, flaxseed and other grains taken out. Then the residue, weed seeds, chaff and stuff of that character is sold for $1.50 a ton. The point I want to make is this: There is no justification for any company doing that, retaining the full value of the broken wheat and such like grains taken out of the first screenings. That is the justifiable complaint that my hon. friends to my left and the farmers they represent in the West have. [DOT] I pointed out in 1919 and in 1920 in the House, as well as on other occasions, that it was an injustice to the farmer. It was a loss of valuable grains which belonged to him, and he had a right to complain. I think that we ought to find some way, and we had this in mind a little over a year ago when the other commission was working upon this, of so adjusting the regulations and controlling the terminal elevators that the farmer would get the full value of these screenings.
There is another feature. According to the law, when a dockage is made the shipper or farmer gets the value or warehouse receipt for the wheat less the dockage. When the dockage is ascertained the shipper is supposed to get credit for that. Now- through ignorance very frequently, and when I say ignorance I mean simply ignorance of his rights, the shipper does not claim that credit, and it has not been made obligatory upon the elevator actually to make the entry and advise him of ' it. In other words, a great many elevators take the stand; It is there, if they like to claim it, well and good. But if they do not know enough to claim it they do not get it. That is one complaint the farmers have which should be corrected by regulation.
Then next is this, and it is even more important. I have already cited the process of a second cleaning. What the shipper or the farmer is entitled to from the elevator is the full value of the screenings from the first cleaning, less, of course, the charges for cleaning, which charges are fixed by the schedule. He is entitled to the full value, but he does not get it. That is the point I want to make, and I would suggest that these references of mine, perhaps imperfectly made to-night, should be brought to the attention of whoever is going to investigate the matter and a serious effort be made to adjust that problem.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Does the complaint apply only to the government elevator's? Does it not apply also to the Saskatchewan Elevator Company?

To all elevators. I will speak with absolute positiveness up to 1919. It included all elevators at the head of the lakes up to that time. I cannot speak with the same positiveness since, because since 1920 I have not personally checked up the figures, but I know that the conditions are the same; there has been no change. I asked some questions in the House the other da}'. I am not in a position nor do I wish to weary the House with any detailed analysis of these questions and answers-
The remarks my hon. friend has just made do not apply to the mixing elevators, do they?

No, because the mixing
elevator must own its grain. It purchases it outright. I am referring to the public terminal elevators. I could name them. I have a list, but my hon. friend knows them. It is practically all the elevators at the head of the lakes, those known as public terminal elevators operating under license from the Grain Commission. The mixing or private elevator purchases' its grain outright, and of course once in full possession of it, it can do what it likes with it. I do not want my hon. friend to think for a moment I am discussing now the question of whether it is advisable to permit mixing. I know the problem and would be prepared to discuss it, but I do not think it is germane to this question.
I asked certain questions which will be found on Hansard on page 1661. One was this:
What is the information as applied to public terminal elevators and the government elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur:-(a) Total amount of wheat scalpings shipped from same: (b) total amount of oats scalpings shipped from same.
The answer to that is this, and I want to submit to the minister that I am not particularly complaining about the answer other than to say that I feel that more accurate information ought to be in the possession of the commission or the department:
The board is unable to furnish the amount of wheat or oat scalpings shipped or received as they are included in the records of the board as elevator scalpings. In consequence no separate record is available showing the composition or quantities of either wheat or oat scalpings handled by terminal elevators.
Frankly I question the correctness of the answer. If it is correct, I would suggest that some record be kept of these important matters? I also asked this question:

(c) Total amount of second recleaned scalpings shipped from same.
To which the answer was:
From public terminal elevators, 3,705 tons; from government elevators, 633 tons.
From further answers it will be noted that there were 7,000 tons and 44,000 tons, showing that there is a very large quantity of these screenings and scalpings dealt with by the elevators.
What I am going to say now is not assertive; I am not in a position to assert, and yet I am fully satisfied in my own mind that it is the case. The cream or the valuable grain seeds in these screenings is appropriated by the elevator companies, and pooled by them and shipped, to Minneapolis. I wish the minister would note what I say in that regard. I want just simply to assert that as in my opinion correct, without having under my hand proof. The minister will find if he will request his commission to make an investigation that what I say is true. If it is true, then it is not a square deal to the shipper; that is all there is to it.
Let me turn to another phase of this elevator question, and again I do not advance what I am going to say in the way of an attack on the elevator companies so much as an argument on the question of system. Under the Grain Act the grain commissioners fix a charge for the use of the elevators-for the elevating of the grain, for fifteen days storage, and so forth. Now, under the figures that I gave this House, over a period of years, it was shown that the elevators got a return on capital invested of about 8 per cent without taking into consideration either overages or screenings. Plus screenings, and leaving out overages, their return amounted to about 13 per cent. Taking an average through, including overages, their return ran into enormous sums which varied and went as high as 75 or 80 per cent-very high earnings. Now, what I am getting at is this: Those screenings, did not properly, in equity, belong to the elevators. They may by the distortion of the law, perhaps, establish an ownership; but I want to say that in the spirit and intent of the law, and in equity, they did not properly belong to them. That being the case, I am perfectly sure of my ground in that regard, what I am getting at is this: If the elevator companies can show that if they are deprived of the revenue from screenings they cannot earn what is a reasonable return, then it is the duty of the Grain Commissioners to fix their fees so that they can earn a reasonable return. But I know this, that if you add the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
overages to the returns by fees their earnings are not only sufficient but very very large. I argued in 1919 and 1920, and I argue to-night, that the duty of the grain board is to fix the elevator fees at a figure that will give to the elevators a proper return for the services they render, whatever that may be decided upon; but in so far as the overages and the screenings are concerned, they should not be permitted to become a part of the revenue of the elevator companies.
JVlr. BROWN: If I understand rightly there was an amendment to the Grain Act that allowed the government to appropriate all over a certain percentage of the overages. Is that being carried out?
As far as I know it is.
Then, of course, the overages cannot now be anything like they were in former days.
I am glad my hon. friend-

Before my hon. friend deals with that, I should like to mention that the government owns but a very limited percentage of the storage at Fort William and Port Arthur; there is a large part of it owned by the men who ship grain there from co-operative companies.

I want the minister to realize that I am not directing this as against government operation at all but against the
system.
The elevator system?

Against the whole elevator system, the control and handling of grain at the head of the lakes. In answer to my hon. friend for Lisgnr (Mr. Brown) I may say that in 1919 I brought to the attention of the House this frightful abuse of privilege, and I showed by figures definitely how these overages were made up and the enormous quantity. I showed, I think, beyond contradiction-in fact the figures were never questioned

that something over $15,000,000 worth of grain in the preceding few years had been appropriated at that time contrary to the act. I took the stand at that time that I take tonight-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is that in overages?

In overages. I took the stand then, and I take it to-night, that we as a parliament should never have allowed the elevators to retain those overages. I am aware the elevators will say, "Oh, we are making a shortage and we require overages to make up the shortages." But the figures I gave were the net figures, after allowing them to cover their shortage. As a matter of fact, the amount of shortage returned is only a modicum of the amount of overage that yearly accrues, and if the House, or any member interested, will take the two, from 1912 down to the present time, the last 11 years, I venture to say the shortage will not amount to two per cent of the overages so that it is a negligible quantity. Well, I argued that those overages should not be allowed to be retained by the elevator companies, and I showed at that time that the permission to retain them was in itself an inducement to create the overages-
Hear, hear.

That- was the crux of the whole business, and that was why I sought to have the law, as it was then, observed, because according to the law they were not permitted to have them. However, in 1919 the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), Mr. Maharg, then member for Maple Creek, Mr. Reid, then member for Mackenzie, and some other hon. gentlemen questioned the advisability of the stand I took and they attacked me. Well, I am of rather a forgiving and merciful nature; I desire to forget those things. Anyway, they took exception to my stand and they made this declaration: They said that speaking for the farmers of the prairies they felt there was no particular abuse in that regard, and they suggested that one-half of one per cent should be permitted to the elevator companies. Well, that did not seem very much and when one says it quickly, without giving it any thought, one-half of one per cent sounds a pretty small quantity. But now what do we find? We find this: Not only do they retain one-half of one per cent, but there is an impression that they do something else. The one-hal. of one per cent has no basis in law or in equity; it is simply an arbitrary figure fixed; there was no logic in fixing it and no reason; there were no previous figures on which it could be based; there were no lack of earnings on which it could be based-there was absolutely no basis for it at all but an arbitrary basis. Well, they not only take their one-half of one per cent, but there is a grave suspicion that some at least-I will not say all by any means

(hat some at least treat the excess, or much of the excess ab; ve the one-half of one per cent in other ways more devious and dark than visible, and the practice of dockage is going on to almost as great an extent, I think, as ever. Therefore, when this commission sits



Supply-Trade and Commerce
I believe the main question for it to consider is the making of such regulations, and the providing of such fees, as will remove this abuse and remove the temptation

shall I say?-the inducement to extract from the grain at the head of the lakes this illegal tribute-or inequitable tribute because it is made legal by the amendment I referred to.
But that is not all. You have got to go further back than that. You have got to go back to the country elevator and you have also got to meet a similar situation there because, as anybody knows, the grain is frequently either bought outright there or, if it is not, a dockage is made on the country elevators. So that the commission has a very important duty to perform, and I believe this: It will be found, without very much trouble, that a substantial increase of the return can be given to the shipper; and after all when you take into consideration this great problem-and I think that most of us realize that it is one of the most gigantic problems we have facing the commercial life of this country-after all there is no short cut to the increase of value to the farmers of the plains; there is no mystic wand that you can wave to get them a higher price for their wheat. You are going to get a higher price for the farm products of the prairies by lowering the cost of moving the goods to the seaboard, more perhaps than in any other way, and it does not matter so much whether that is in the way of lowering freight rates, or lowering of handling charges, or what not, but what I do say is this: we have got to check every detail of the process, and it is quite an expensive process.
You take your grain from your threshing machine, you haul it to the country elevator, and there is a certain amount of leakage, shrinkage, and such like, and fees charged for. It is shipped then to the terminal, and there is a certain amount of dockage, transfer fees and so on. It comes down the lakes and is retransferred at Port Colborne or some other point, and there you have another charge. It goes to Montreal, and must be loaded from the ship, transferred to the elevator there, and after that, if you follow the thing through, and you have charges for warehouse receipts, bank interest discount and insurance, it will soon mount up to a measurable margin between what it brings in the ultimate market and what is received by the farmer. So that the duty of the department, and what we were trying to get at two years ago through the commission which was appointed, and what I hope we will accomplish by the next commission, is to so check over the process so that the actual cost will be reduced to a minimum,

safeguarding the' legitimate rights of those doing the business, but that every measure of waste that is now going on, every shrinkage, every, dockage that is not absolutely essential shall be eliminated, and where any dockage is made that every pound that belongs to the farmer shall go back to him.
Take a carload of wheat of, say, 1,000 bushels; there is a 5 per cent dockage which means 50 bushels. Fifty bushels in comparison with 1,000 bushels is very small, but there is no reason why it should be ignored. Or, we will take it another way. Suppose that out of that 50 bushels there are 30 bushels of good grain-and I believe I am about right in suggesting that that is the case in most intsances-that 30 bushels of good grain may be cracked or it may be this, that and the other, it may not be No. 1, but it will be, at least available for first class feed. That is of value to the farmer. It might only represent a few dollars and may not seem a very serious matter, but when you add to that, as I have already pointed out, a little shrinkage here and a little overcharge there, it means a big thing in the long run and in the aggregate to the farming community.
In the hon. member's opinion are the elevators entitled to any dockage whatever?

The hour is getting late and I really do not want to pursue the subject. I will say no. In making that categorical answer, I am quite aware that I am opening up quite a field of discussion, but the point I have been endeavouring to make-and I think it ought to be the objective of any inquiry-is that the elevators are entitled to a fair remuneration for the services rendered. That remuneration ought to be fixed for them under the Grain Act. It is always a dangerous thing, I do not care what business it is, to permit any person to have the privilege of extracting a portion of a commodity handled as a part of his fees for handling it, whether it is wheat or any other commodity. It is not done in any other line. You do not let the railway company take part of the goods as a fee for transportation. We fix a rate for them to charge. We do not let a railway company take part of a carload of wheat to pay for possible losses on the trip. We say to them "You deliver that cargo at the head of the lakes, and deliver it at so much a hundred pounds." That is all they will get. I do not see why an elevator company, which is a common carrier, should have any different method of remuneration than a railway company, because both are common carriers.

Sup-ply-Trade and Commerce
There is this difference, that there is a loss in weight in handling grain that must be provided for.
There is a loss in weight in transportation.
You would not approve of the regulation of the grain commission whereby, in the case of a car carrying 3 per cent dockage, the elevator remunerates itself by taking the 3 per cent.
I do not think it is fair to the shipper at all.
It is a question of toll or money charge.

Let me put it in this way if you ship a car load of goods to a man, it may be boots or shoes or anything else-let us forget wheat for a minute-and he has the privilege of dealing with those goods, and of retaining for himself a certain quantity, say
3 per cent, he is going to see that he gets the 3 per cent, if he can. If there is any possibility of him getting it, he is going to get it. If you eliminate that feature you eliminate the temptation to him of extracting anything.
I shall direct the attention of the commission to the remarks of my hon. friend.
What is the status of the Manitoba litigation in regard tc the Grain Act?
It is before the court.
Item agreed to.

There are some steamship subventions not yet voted, but perhaps we might adjourn now.
Progress reported.
